name: Learn: Supply Chain Security
description: Secure the image supply chain step by step — scan images with Trivy, run static manifest analysis with kubesec, pin images by sha256 digest, enforce an approved registry with a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, and ban the :latest tag. Exam-focused supply-chain practice on real nodes.
objective: CKS › Supply Chain Security (20%). Goal: scan images for CVEs with Trivy, statically analyze manifests with kubesec, pin images by @sha256 digest, enforce an approved registry via a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy + binding, and ban :latest — the supply-chain tasks the exam weights heavily.

questions.title: Scan an image with Trivy
questions.teach:
**Trivy** (by Aqua Security) scans container images for known **CVEs** in OS packages and language dependencies. On the exam you often run it as a one-shot **Job** inside the cluster and read the report from the pod logs.

`trivy image <ref>` pulls the image, matches every installed package against vulnerability databases, and prints a table ending with a `Total:` line per target. A completed Job with that output in its logs is your proof the scan ran.

**Common Trivy invocations:**
- `trivy image <ref>` — scan a container image (the exam classic).
- `trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL <ref>` — only show the severities you care about.
- `trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL <ref>` — non-zero exit when matches found (CI gating).
- `trivy image --ignore-unfixed <ref>` — hide CVEs with no fix available.
- `trivy fs <dir>` / `trivy config <dir>` / `trivy k8s` — filesystem, IaC/misconfig, and live-cluster scanning.

**Running it as a Job — the gotchas:**
- Jobs **must** set `restartPolicy: Never` or `OnFailure` (never the default `Always`) — the API rejects it otherwise.
- `kubectl create job ... -- image busybox:1.36` puts everything after `--` into **args**; the first token (`image`) is Trivy's subcommand, not a flag.
- Read results with `kubectl logs job/<name>` (or `logs -l job-name=<name>`); use `kubectl wait --for=condition=complete` to block until done.
- Set a sane `backoffLimit`; a failed scan (e.g. DB download fails offline) retries and can look stuck. Trivy needs network to fetch its vuln DB on first run.
- `--exit-code` controls Trivy's process exit, which maps to whether the Job **Complete**s or **Fail**s — don't gate the pass on CVEs being present/absent.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `cks-supply`, create a **Job** named `trivy-scan` that runs image `aquasec/trivy:latest` with args `image busybox:1.36` to scan the busybox image. Let it run to completion.

Target: Job `trivy-scan` reaches `Complete` and its pod logs contain Trivy CVE output (a `Total:` / vulnerabilities summary).
questions.hint: `kubectl create job trivy-scan -n cks-supply --image=aquasec/trivy:latest -- image busybox:1.36`, then `kubectl -n cks-supply wait --for=condition=complete job/trivy-scan --timeout=180s` and `kubectl -n cks-supply logs job/trivy-scan`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: trivy-scan
  namespace: cks-supply
spec:
  backoffLimit: 2
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: trivy
        image: aquasec/trivy:latest
        args: ["image", "busybox:1.36"]
YAML
kubectl -n cks-supply wait --for=condition=complete job/trivy-scan --timeout=180s
kubectl -n cks-supply logs job/trivy-scan

verification.description: Job trivy-scan completed and produced Trivy CVE output

questions.title: Static analysis with kubesec
questions.teach:
**kubesec** performs **static security analysis** of Kubernetes manifests — it scores a pod/deployment YAML and tells you which `securityContext` hardening is missing (runAsNonRoot, dropped capabilities, read-only root fs, resource limits, etc.).

Unlike Trivy (which scans *images*), kubesec scans the *manifest* before it ever reaches the cluster. Run it as a Job with `controlplaneio/kubesec:latest scan /path/manifest.yaml`; the logs contain a JSON report with a numeric `score` and a list of `advise`/`critical` points.

**Ways to feed kubesec a manifest (it needs the YAML *inside* the container):**
- **ConfigMap volume** (this task): put the manifest in a ConfigMap, mount it at `/manifests`, pass `scan /manifests/pod.yaml`. Each ConfigMap key becomes a file; use `subPath` if you must land a single key at an exact filename.
- **emptyDir + initContainer** that writes the file, shared with the kubesec container.
- **stdin / HTTP API**: locally `kubesec scan pod.yaml` or `cat pod.yaml | kubesec scan -`; kubesec can also run as an HTTP server (`kubesec http 8080`) you POST YAML to.

**Gotchas:**
- It is *static* — a high score means a well-hardened manifest, it does **not** mean the image is CVE-free (that's Trivy's job). The two are complementary.
- kubesec exits **non-zero when the score is below threshold**, so a Job can land in **Failed** even though the scan ran correctly — grade on the report in the logs, not the Job condition, or use `restartPolicy: Never` + a generous `backoffLimit`.
- The ConfigMap/volume mount is read-only; the args must match the mounted path exactly (`/manifests/pod.yaml`), not the host path.
- Mounted ConfigMap files update live if the ConfigMap changes, but the Job reads once at startup.
questions.prompt:
A pod manifest is mounted at `/manifests/pod.yaml` via a ConfigMap (already created by setup). In `cks-supply`, create a **Job** named `kubesec-scan` using image `controlplaneio/kubesec:latest` with args `scan /manifests/pod.yaml`, mounting that ConfigMap at `/manifests`. Let it complete.

Target: Job `kubesec-scan` reaches `Complete` and its pod logs contain a kubesec report (a `score` field).
questions.hint: Mount the `kubesec-manifest` ConfigMap at `/manifests`. Args must be `["scan","/manifests/pod.yaml"]`. Then `kubectl -n cks-supply wait --for=condition=complete job/kubesec-scan --timeout=180s` and read the logs.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: kubesec-scan
  namespace: cks-supply
spec:
  backoffLimit: 2
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
      - name: kubesec
        image: controlplaneio/kubesec:latest
        args: ["scan", "/manifests/pod.yaml"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: m
          mountPath: /manifests
      volumes:
      - name: m
        configMap:
          name: kubesec-manifest
YAML
kubectl -n cks-supply wait --for=condition=complete job/kubesec-scan --timeout=180s
kubectl -n cks-supply logs job/kubesec-scan

verification.description: Job kubesec-scan completed and produced a score/report

questions.title: Pin an image by digest (@sha256:)
questions.teach:
A tag like `:1.36` is **mutable** — whoever controls the registry can repoint it to a different, possibly malicious, image. A **digest** (`@sha256:`) is the cryptographic hash of the exact image content, so it is **immutable**: the kubelet pulls precisely the bytes you reviewed, or fails. Pinning by digest (`image: busybox@sha256:<64 hex>`) is the strongest integrity guarantee for the supply chain and is preferred over tags for trusted workloads. **Ways to reference an image (weakest → strongest):** - `busybox` — no tag, **implicitly `:latest`**; worst case, unreproducible. - `busybox:1.36` — explicit tag; readable but still mutable (the tag can be moved). - `busybox:1.36@sha256:` — tag **and** digest; human-readable yet pinned to exact bytes (digest wins if they disagree). - `busybox@sha256:` — pure digest; fully immutable. - Repeat the pattern with a full registry path: `registry.k8s.io/pause@sha256:`. **Finding a digest:** - `crane digest busybox:1.36` or `skopeo inspect docker://busybox:1.36` (look for `Digest`). - `docker buildx imagetools inspect busybox:1.36`. - After a pull, `kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].imageID}'` shows the resolved digest (`imageID`), while `.spec...image` keeps what you wrote. **Gotchas:** - The digest is a sha256 over the **manifest**, so multi-arch images have a different digest per architecture — a digest copied from another arch won't pull on your node. - `imagePullPolicy` defaults to `IfNotPresent` for digests/fixed tags but `Always` for `:latest` — another reason `:latest` is discouraged. - Combining a wrong tag with a right digest still pulls the digest; the tag is cosmetic. - Digest-pinned images skip the "pull newest" convenience: you must re-pin to upgrade.
questions.prompt:
In `cks-supply`, create a pod `digest-pod` whose container image is pinned **by digest** — use `busybox@sha256:<digest>` (any valid busybox sha256 digest), running `sleep 3600`.

Target: pod `digest-pod` exists and its container `image` field contains `@sha256:` (not a plain tag).
questions.hint: Find a digest with `crane digest busybox:1.36` or `docker buildx imagetools inspect busybox:1.36`, or reuse a known one. Then set `image: busybox@sha256:<64-hex-digest>` in the pod spec. The check only requires the image field to contain `@sha256:`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: digest-pod
  namespace: cks-supply
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox@sha256:9ae97d36d26566ff84e8893c64a6dc4fe8ca6d1144bf5b87b2b85a32def253c7
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
YAML

verification.description: digest-pod image is pinned by @sha256: digest

questions.title: Approved-registry admission (ValidatingAdmissionPolicy)
questions.teach:
A **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP)** enforces rules in-cluster using **CEL** expressions — no webhook server to run. It has two parts: the **policy** (the CEL rule) and a **binding** that says which objects it applies to.

A classic supply-chain control is an **approved-registry** allowlist: reject any pod whose container images don't start with a trusted registry such as `registry.k8s.io/`. The CEL walks `object.spec.containers` and checks `image.startsWith('registry.k8s.io/')`. The policy only takes effect once a **ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding** references it.

**The three moving parts:**
- **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy** — `matchConstraints.resourceRules` (which apiGroups/resources/operations it watches) + `validations[].expression` (the CEL that must be *true* to admit). Optional: `failurePolicy` (`Fail`/`Ignore`), `variables`, `matchConditions`, `paramKind`.
- **ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding** — `policyName`, `validationActions` (`Deny`, `Warn`, `Audit` — combinable), and `matchResources` to narrow scope (e.g. by namespace label). Empty `matchResources: {}` = everything the policy matches.
- Optional **param object** (via `paramKind` + `paramRef` in the binding) to parameterize the rule (e.g. a ConfigMap listing allowed registries).

**CEL helpers for image checks:**
- All containers: `object.spec.containers.all(c, c.image.startsWith('registry.k8s.io/'))`.
- Don't forget **initContainers** and **ephemeralContainers** — a full policy ANDs all three lists; checking only `containers` is the classic miss.
- Ban `:latest`: `object.spec.containers.all(c, !c.image.endsWith(':latest'))`.

**Gotchas:**
- The policy does **nothing** until a binding references it — two objects, always.
- VAP is cluster-scoped and GA in v1.30; older clusters need the feature gate / webhooks instead. It's a drop-in alternative to OPA Gatekeeper / Kyverno with no extra pod.
- `validationActions: [Deny]` blocks on admission; `Warn`/`Audit` only surface messages — pick `Deny` to actually enforce.
- `failurePolicy: Fail` blocks the request if CEL errors (e.g. a null field); `Ignore` lets it through — safer to validate fields exist first via `matchConditions`.
- CEL runs at admission only, so **pre-existing** non-compliant pods are untouched.
questions.prompt:
Create a **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy** named `approved-registry` that denies Pods whose container images do **not** start with `registry.k8s.io/`, and a **ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding** named `approved-registry-binding` that enables it (action `Deny`) on Pods.

Target: both objects exist; the policy's CEL validation references `registry.k8s.io` over `object.spec.containers`, and the binding references policy `approved-registry`.
questions.hint: `matchConstraints` on resource `pods` (apiGroups: [""]). Validation CEL: `object.spec.containers.all(c, c.image.startsWith('registry.k8s.io/'))`. Create the binding with `policyName: approved-registry`, `validationActions: [Deny]`, and an empty `matchResources: {}`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: approved-registry
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations: ["CREATE","UPDATE"]
      resources: ["pods"]
  validations:
  - expression: "object.spec.containers.all(c, c.image.startsWith('registry.k8s.io/'))"
    message: "images must come from registry.k8s.io"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: approved-registry-binding
spec:
  policyName: approved-registry
  validationActions: ["Deny"]
  matchResources: {}
YAML

verification.description: VAP approved-registry + binding exist with the registry.k8s.io rule

questions.title: Ban the :latest tag (pin a real version)
questions.teach:
`:latest` is the worst tag for supply-chain integrity: it floats to whatever was pushed last, so two deploys of the "same" image can run different code — unreproducible and un-auditable. Policy and CIS benchmarks require an **explicit version tag** (e.g. `:1.25-alpine`) or, better, a **digest**.

Always pin to a concrete tag or `@sha256:` so rollbacks and scans refer to exactly one image.

**What counts as `:latest`:**
- `nginx` (no tag) resolves to `nginx:latest` — an **untagged** image is just as bad as an explicit `:latest`.
- `nginx:latest` — explicit and equally mutable.
- Acceptable: `nginx:1.25-alpine`, or pinned by digest `nginx@sha256:<hex>`.
- Side effect: `:latest` forces `imagePullPolicy: Always`; a fixed tag/digest defaults to `IfNotPresent`.

**Ways to enforce "no :latest":**
- Admission: a `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` / Kyverno / Gatekeeper rule (`!image.endsWith(':latest')` and also reject untagged images).
- Scanning: kubesec/Trivy/`conftest` in CI flag `:latest` in manifests before apply.

**Deployment gotchas (relevant here):**
- `kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.25-alpine` sets the image; editing it later triggers a **RollingUpdate** (default strategy: `maxSurge 25%`, `maxUnavailable 25%`) — `Recreate` is the alternative that kills old pods first.
- Changing only the image is a rollout you can inspect/undo: `kubectl rollout status/history/undo deploy/web` (`--to-revision=N`); `revisionHistoryLimit` caps stored revisions.
- `--record` is deprecated — use a `kubernetes.io/change-cause` annotation to label a revision.
- Scaling (`kubectl scale`) does **not** create a new revision; only template changes (like the image) do.
questions.prompt:
In `cks-supply`, create a **Deployment** named `web` (1 replica) whose container image uses a **pinned version** — NOT `:latest` and NOT an untagged image. For example `nginx:1.25-alpine` (or any explicit tag / digest).

Target: Deployment `web` exists and its container image is not `:latest` and carries an explicit tag or `@sha256:` digest.
questions.hint: `kubectl create deployment web -n cks-supply --image=nginx:1.25-alpine`. Avoid `nginx` (implicit latest) and `nginx:latest`.
questions.solution:
kubectl create deployment web -n cks-supply --image=nginx:1.25-alpine
kubectl -n cks-supply get deploy web -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'

verification.description: Deployment web uses a pinned version, not :latest
